name: Modular monolith with a separate triage service
summary: Relay's service and its escalation worker stay one artifact with one database, as in Option A. Triage moves into its own deployable service with its own database; Relay's service calls it over the internal network to queue tickets and read suggestions.

components.name: Browsers, API clients and the support inbox
Relay database: tasks, rules; tables owned by modules
triage-svc: queue, worker and model adapter

flows.data: ticket text out; suggested labels back
escalation emails: link, priority, rule, step; never the title

boundaries.TB5: Relay service to triage-svc on the internal network

ESC-N01: Suggestions come back over an API, and Relay must store them as suggestions only: a rule kept at the boundary between two codebases, checked by a contract test rather than one module.
ESC-N03: Rules stay in the monolith with relay.roles and one audit table; triage-svc needs its own service authentication, but holds no rules.
ESC-N04: The flood cap stays in the monolith's one database, counted and sent in one transaction.
ESC-N05: Target validation lives in one module, as in Option A.
ESC-N06: A rule change and its notification are written in one transaction, as in Option A.
ESC-N07: Task titles stay in the monolith; only ticket text crosses TB5 to triage-svc.
ESC-N09: The step path is Option A's; triage-svc is one more service to watch.
ESC-N10: No broker; escalation calls only email and webhook delivery.
CON-1: Two deployables and two databases for one rota: workable, but triage-svc needs its own pipeline, dashboards and runbook.
CON-2: Two artifacts on the train; a change to the triage API needs both deployed in order.
CON-3: The limiter stays in Relay's service, as in Option A.
CON-4: Relay's service queues the ticket at triage-svc and returns 202; no request waits for the model.
CON-5: Webhook sends stay jobs with idempotency keys in the monolith.
CON-6: triage-svc scales on its own, without scaling the monolith.
